head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Treats each soldier j as the MIDDLE of a team
Fix the middle element of a triple
Left smaller / left greater: soldiers before j with smaller / larger ratings (`lg = j - ls` since ratings are distinct)
Increasing teams: a smaller one on the left and a larger one on the right
Decreasing teams: larger on the left and smaller on the right

p: `[2,5,3,4,1]`: contribution of each middle soldier:
A team is a triple i < j < k that is increasing or decreasing. With j fixed, the choices for i and k are independent, so the count is a product. The O(n³) triple loop becomes an O(n²) count.

bullets: Space: O(1). A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) lowers it to O(n log n).

1395.takeaway: Fix the middle soldier and multiply (smaller-left × greater-right) + (greater-left × smaller-right).

Start value s needs s + lowest ≥ 1, so s = 1 − lowest

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: stage = {c: i for i, c in enumerate('croak')}
Letter → its position in the word
Frogs currently at stage i (last said letter i of 'croak')
Counting items in each phase of a pipeline
A 'c' starts a new croak; either a free frog or a new frog
A letter appears with no frog ready for it: invalid string
'k' finishes a croak and frees the frog for reuse
The most frogs croaking at the same time is the minimum number of frogs needed

p: `"crcoakroak"` (counts are for stages c, r, o, a, k):
bullets: Answer: 2, and it ends with active = 0 (all croaks complete).

blocks.h: Why is the maximum of active frogs the answer?
p: Each frog can do one croak at a time but can start another after finishing. So the number of frogs needed equals the largest number of overlapping unfinished croaks.

1419.takeaway: Count frogs at each stage of 'croak'; the peak number of unfinished croaks is the answer.

blocks.h: Why is this better than a binary search per row?
p: Binary search per row costs O(rows · log cols) calls. The staircase walk costs at most rows + cols calls because each call moves either left or down, which matters when `get` calls are limited.

1428.takeaway: Staircase from the top-right: move left on a 1, down on a 0.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Hat → people who like it (hats are numbered 1–40, people at most 10)
Number of ways to assign the hats considered so far so that exactly the people in `mask` have hats
for hat in 1..40; for mask descending
Each hat is given to at most one person; descending masks avoid using the same hat twice in a round
Give this hat to person p, who has none yet

p: `hats = [[3,4],[4,5],[5]]`: ways per set of people with hats after each hat (mask bit p = person p):

blocks.h: Why iterate over hats instead of people?
p: There are at most 10 people, so masks have 2^10 states, while hats go up to 40. Looping over hats and choosing at most one person per hat keeps the state small (2^10 × 40 transitions of at most 10 people).

1434.takeaway: Bitmask DP over hats: dp[mask of people already hatted], each hat goes to at most one person who likes it.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Adjacency list of the undirected tree
DFS (Depth-First Search) returning the time spent inside u's subtree, with the parent `p` excluded so we do not walk back
Tree traversal without a visited set
Go into the child v only if its subtree has apples (sub > 0) or v itself has one
Walking down and back along the edge to v costs 2, plus the time inside

p: The 7-node tree from the problem; apples at nodes 2, 4, 5. Subtree times in the order the calls finish:
bullets: Answer: 8 (4 edges to visit, each walked twice).

blocks.h: Why count every needed edge twice?
p: We must return to the root, so every edge on a path to an apple is walked down and back: 2 per edge. Edges leading only to apple-free subtrees are skipped.

bullets: Space: O(n) (recursion depth plus the adjacency list).

1443.takeaway: Tree DFS that adds 2 per edge only where the subtree contains an apple.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost to paint houses i.. given the previous house's colour `prev` and `t` neighbourhoods formed so far
DP (Dynamic Programming) state: position, last colour, groups
A new neighbourhood starts exactly when the colour differs from the previous house (`prev = 0` at the start, so house 0 always starts one)
A house that is already painted can only keep its colour
Painting is free for pre-painted houses

p: Five unpainted houses, 2 colours, target 3 neighbourhoods, costs `[[1, 10], [10, 1], [10, 1], [1, 10], [5, 1]]`. The optimal colouring found by the search:
bullets: One optimal plan paints colours 1, 2, 2, 1, 1: groups [1] [2 2] [1 1] (3 neighbourhoods), cost 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 9.

p: Whether the next house starts a new neighbourhood depends only on whether its colour equals the previous house's colour. The DP therefore needs the last colour, not the entire history.

bullets: Time: O(m · n · target · n): states m·n·target, n colour choices each.

1473.takeaway: Memoized DP over (house, previous colour, neighbourhoods so far); a colour change opens a new neighbourhood.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Not enough flowers in total: impossible
Scans left to right counting runs of `k` adjacent flowers that have bloomed by `day`; each full run is one bouquet
Greedy check inside a binary search
run = 0 when a flower is not ready
Bouquets need ADJACENT flowers, so one unbloomed flower breaks the run
The answer is one of the bloom days, so search between the earliest and latest
Enough bouquets by mid: try an earlier day

blocks.h: Why binary search on the day?
p: Waiting longer never reduces the number of bouquets, so feasibility is monotone in the day. The answer is the first day where `can` becomes true.

1482.takeaway: Binary search on the day, with a one-pass greedy that counts runs of k bloomed flowers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Day of the last rain on each lake (that lake is full now)
Sorted list of day indices where no rain falls and a lake can be dried
Index of the first dry day AFTER the lake's previous rain: the earliest day we could have dried it
Finding the first element greater than a value in a sorted list
Uses that dry day to dry this lake, removing it from the free dry days
No dry day exists between the two rains: a flood is unavoidable
Unused dry days dry some lake harmlessly (1 is a valid filler)

head: day
event
note
ans so far
rows: lake 2 is full since day 1: dry it on day 2
lake 1 is full since day 0: dry it on day 3

bullets: Result `[-1, -1, 2, 1, -1, -1]`: day 2 dries lake 2, day 3 dries lake 1.

blocks.h: Why the first dry day after the earlier rain, and why decide late?
p: Drying is only useful between two rains on the same lake. Decisions are made when the second rain arrives (when the need is known), and the earliest dry day after the first rain is chosen so later dry days stay available for other lakes whose windows start later.

bullets: Time: O(n log n): `bisect_right` is O(log n) and `dry.pop(j)` is O(n) in the worst case, so O(n²) worst case.

1488.takeaway: Remember each full lake's last rain; when it rains again, dry it on the earliest dry day after that rain (binary search).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum semesters to finish exactly the courses in mask
All prerequisites of i are inside mask: course i is available
Standard trick to enumerate every non-empty subset of `avail` (in descending order)
At most k courses per semester

p: `n = 4`, prerequisites `2→1, 3→1, 1→4`, `k = 2` (bit i−1 is course i). Minimum semesters to reach each reachable set of finished courses:

blocks.h: Why enumerate subsets of the available courses?
p: Taking fewer than k available courses can matter: finishing a specific course early may unlock others. The DP therefore tries every subset of size at most k of the courses available now, and `(sub - 1) & avail` visits them all in O(2^|avail|).

bullets: Time: O(3^n) over all (mask, subset-of-complement) pairs, fine for n ≤ 15.

1494.takeaway: Bitmask DP: from each finished set, try every subset of at most k available courses as the next semester.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of Euclidean distances from (x, y) to all positions; this function is convex (bowl-shaped)
ternary search on x, inner ternary search on y
Each ternary search cuts the interval to two thirds per step by comparing two interior points; the outer search uses the best y for each x
For a fixed x, the minimum total distance over y
(2/3)^60 shrinks the range of 100 far below 1e-5, enough for the required precision

p: Four points around (1, 1). First outer iterations (x range, then the best total distance found for each probe x):
bullets: After 60 iterations the minimum total distance is `4.0`, at the centre (1, 1).

p: The sum of distances is convex, and the minimum over y of a convex function in (x, y) is again convex in x. A convex function has no local minimum other than the global one, so if f(m1) < f(m2) the minimum cannot lie to the right of m2, and vice versa.

bullets: Time: O(60 · 60 · n): outer and inner iterations times n points.

1515.takeaway: Nested ternary search on a convex sum of distances (geometric median).

Full bottles obtained by exchanging as many sets as possible
Leftover empties plus the empties of the newly drunk bottles

p: `numBottles = 9`, `numExchange = 3`:

blocks.h: Why a loop and not one formula?
p: Each exchange produces new empties that can be exchanged again, so the process repeats until fewer than numExchange empties remain. (A closed form exists: `n + (n - 1) // (e - 1)` = 13 here.)

1518.takeaway: Simulate exchanges: new = empty // k, then empty = empty % k + new, until fewer than k empties.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A list `out` where out[d] = number of leaves at distance d below this node (index 0 unused)
Distance histograms returned up the tree
A leaf is at distance 1 from its parent (distances are measured from the node that receives the list)
L[i] * R[j] when i + j <= distance
Leaf pairs split across the left and right subtrees, joined at this node: distance i + j
Counting pairs through the LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor)
Passing leaves up one edge increases each distance by 1; leaves already at distance `distance` are dropped

p: Tree `[1,2,3,null,4]`, `distance = 3`; internal nodes in post-order (L and R are the histograms from the children):

blocks.h: Why count pairs at the lowest common ancestor?
p: The shortest path between two leaves goes up to their lowest common ancestor and down. Counting pairs only at that ancestor counts each pair exactly once, using the stored distances from each side.

bullets: Space: O(distance) per recursion level, O(h · distance) in total.

1530.takeaway: Return a per-distance histogram of leaves from each subtree; join left and right histograms at the common ancestor.

At least k missing already, so the answer lies before arr[mid]

p: If `lo` array elements are smaller than the answer, then among the numbers up to the answer, `lo` are present and the rest are missing. The k-th missing number is therefore k + lo.

1539.takeaway: Binary search on 'missing count before arr[mid]'; the answer is lo + k.

p: S_n has 2^n − 1 characters, which is exponential. The recursive definition lets us find bit k by following one branch per level, in O(n) time.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A wildcard pattern: the word with position i masked
Replace one character with a wildcard
Another word already produced the same pattern: the two words differ only at position i (or are equal, but words are distinct)

p: `["abcd","acbd","aacd"]`: patterns produced word by word (rows up to the first match):
bullets: `aacd` and an earlier word share the pattern `a*cd`, so the answer is True.

blocks.h: Why is this faster than comparing every pair?
p: Comparing all pairs of n words of length L costs O(n² · L). Each word generates L patterns and a hash set detects collisions, for O(n · L²) time (building each pattern costs O(L)).

bullets: Space: O(n · L²) for the patterns.

1554.takeaway: Mask each position with '*' and look for a pattern seen before; hashing replaces pairwise comparison.
